primitives.name: Oar Blade Positioning
primitives.verbatim_quote: 64 WALTER CAMP'S BOOK OF COLLEGE SPORTS reach he will get his oar into the water at about five to seven feet forward of the thole-pin, and bring it out at finish from four to five feet aft of the tholepin.
primitives.assumptions: Linear oar path approximated by fixed pivot point at thole-pin.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When blade position deviates beyond 1 foot from optimal range.

layer2.mapping: Maps blade displacement to hydrodynamic force vector during stroke cycle.
layer2.telemetry: Blade immersion depth and exit angle.

primitives.name: Outrigger Height Constraint
primitives.verbatim_quote: His outrigger should be high enough above the water, so that his hands comfortably clear his knees on the recover, with oar-blade four inches above the water, or about 71 to 81 inches above his seat.
primitives.assumptions: Hand clearance is required for full recovery motion without drag.
primitives.breakdown_regime: If outrigger too low, hand contacts knee during recovery phase.

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to arm extension constraint in biomechanical kinematics.

primitives.name: Slide Length and Pitch
primitives.verbatim_quote: The seat is, according to the man, from six to nine inches from the bottom of the boat, and the slide from fifteen to twenty inches in length.
primitives.assumptions: Slide length determines range of motion; pitch affects angular alignment.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Exceeds 20 inches or less than 15 inches causes mechanical inefficiency.

layer2.mapping: Determines effective stroke length and angular velocity of oar during pull.
layer2.telemetry: Slide travel distance and angular deviation from vertical.

Rowing stroke mechanics involve a sequence of kinematic transformations governed by fixed geometric relationships between oar, seat, and boat. The oar blade positioning defines the active propulsion zone, where the blade enters water five to seven feet forward of the thole-pin and exits four to five feet aft. These distances define a consistent stroke arc, which is constrained by the slide mechanism's length and pitch. A longer slide allows greater reach, but requires precise pitch adjustment to maintain balance. Outrigger height ensures hand clearance during recovery, preventing drag and maintaining rhythm. Shorter athletes require elevated seats and more aft positioning to compensate for reduced leverage, thus increasing their effective stroke length. The stroke itself is composed of three phases: catch, pull-through, and finish, each defined by specific spatial and temporal boundaries. Recovery mirrors this structure, involving feathering, carrying back, and repositioning. These components form a closed-loop system where mechanical efficiency depends on minimizing energy loss through misalignment or improper timing. Failure modes include blade slippage due to incorrect entry angle, excessive drag from insufficient outrigger height, or loss of momentum from improper slide usage.
